## Where This Fits
At the end of W3 we had a usable loss with two holes in it. CTC's outputs are independent of one another (homophones can only be guessed from acoustics), and the encoder itself — the box that turns $\mathbf{X}$ into $\mathbf{y}^t$ — was never discussed. This week fills both holes and treats **causality**, a constraint that runs through the whole course, formally for the first time. Three protagonists. The **Transformer / Conformer** is the box itself: self-attention lets every frame see the whole utterance, and the convolution module puts the local inductive bias back. The **RNN-T** adds a prediction network to CTC's lattice, giving the output side an autoregressive dependency while staying monotonic and streamable — W3 said "that price is only paid back by the RNN-T in W4", and this is where it is paid. **Attention as a third kind of alignment** (AED, from LAS onwards) fills the column W3's comparison table left blank: soft, non-monotonic, and — the most important correction of the week — **an attention weight is not an estimate of the alignment**.

Where the three course-long axes sit this week. **Latency:** W1 wrote $D_{\text{alg}} = \ell\Delta + \alpha C\Delta$ as a statement; this week supplies the mechanism. Lookahead **accumulates layer by layer** (each layer looks $r_k$ frames to the right, $m = \sum_k r_k$); the wait inside a chunk **does not accumulate** (every layer shares the same chunk boundary), and that difference drives the design of streaming architectures. Two further terms appear that W1 did not have: the **delay a model learns on its own** (the RNN-T's emission delay), and the KV cache, a computational delay that grows linearly with $T$. **Representation:** the subsampling factor $s$ at the front of the encoder fixes $T$, and so fixes how tight W3's bound $T \geq U + r$ is; the RNN-T can emit several symbols per frame, so that bound disappears and is replaced by a compute constraint. W2 asked "who decides the frame rate"; this week the answer first becomes a design parameter you can turn. **Supervision:** the RNN-T and CTC use the same kind of data (audio paired with a transcript), but FastEmit shows that **latency itself can be written into the training objective** — the first precedent for W12's treatment of turn-taking as a learnable decision.

The RNN-T's per-frame binary decision — emit or do not emit — is the direct ancestor of turn-taking modelling in W12, and W13's multi-stream tokenisation in Moshi relies on the same idea of "several symbols may share one time step". On the local-language thread: W3 marked "Mandarin homophones make conditional independence bite harder" as my judgement; this week gives it a mechanism, because the prediction network is an output-side language model. And a character-level Mandarin vocabulary pushes the RNN-T's $T \times U \times |\mathcal{V}'|$ tensor straight into the memory wall — exactly the case the pruned RNN-T paper names in its abstract.

## Learning Objectives
1. Write down the dimension flow of scaled dot-product and multi-head attention ($\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}$ are each $T \times d_k$; the score matrix is $T \times T$), write the streaming mask formally, and explain the division of labour between convolution and self-attention inside a Conformer block, as well as why relative positional encoding becomes necessary under chunking or recurrence.
2. Define the RNN-T output lattice $(t, u)$, write its forward recursion and $P(\ell \mid \mathbf{X}) = \alpha(T, U)\,\varnothing(T, U)$, read the gradient as "node-occupancy times softmax, minus the edge posterior" — a generalisation of W3's $y - \gamma$ — and compare the path sets of RNN-T and CTC (exactly one symbol per frame vs. zero or more; $\binom{T+U-1}{U}$ paths vs. a set constrained by $T \geq U + r$).
3. List the four families of techniques that turn a non-causal encoder into a streaming one (causal mask, chunk-wise attention with lookahead, memory / state carry-over, latency-controlled BLSTM-style), state for each which term the algorithmic delay comes from ($m\,s\Delta$ or $\alpha C\,s\Delta$) and whether it accumulates across layers, and identify emission delay as a third kind of latency that lives outside the architecture.
4. Compute the memory of a KV cache ($2\,n_{\text{layer}}\, d\, T$ numbers) and its per-step cost $O(n_{\text{layer}}\, d\, T)$, and explain why spoken dialogue measured in minutes needs bounded state (sliding windows, memory banks, state-space models).
5. Diagnose "attention is not alignment": explain why the encoder has already mixed context into every position, so the decoder can read the right content without sharp attention; and state that Whisper's word timestamps actually come from dynamic time warping over a small selected subset of cross-attention heads, not from attention as a whole.

## Demos
All three of this week's demos are programs; they are published so that you can read them, re-run them, and change them — **you are not required to run anything**. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slides | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Demo 1 · the RNN-T lattice: paths vs. forward, and `max_symbols_per_step`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos/w04_d1_rnnt_lattice) | p29, p31, p33, p34 | Terminal only. Every RNN-T path for "ab" / "aa" at $T = 1, 2, 3$ with the CTC count beside it ("aa" at $T = 1$: RNN-T 1, CTC 0); a random $\mathbf{y}^{t,u}$ summed over paths and run through the forward recursion cell by cell ($P = 0.008173862970686905$, difference $0.0$, every anti-diagonal $\sum\alpha\beta = P$); then greedy decoding on a *synthetic* joint with and without a cap of 5 symbols per frame — with the cap `"bababab"` and $[1, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0]$ emits per frame, without it frame 3 never stops | standard library (+ `numpy` via the shared helpers) | anything |
| [Demo 2 · one streaming transducer, three chunk sizes](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos/w04_d2_stream_chunks) | p42 | The W3 sentence fed at real-time pace to `sherpa-onnx`'s streaming zipformer in 320 / 640 / 1280 ms chunks; each symbol gets three clocks (encoder frame, audio fed, wall) against the word's acoustic end from W3's forced alignment. Rehearsal: emission delay 220 ms in all three runs, frame for frame; `fed − emit` 500 / 640 / 960 ms against the predicted $c + F/2$ = 480 / 640 / 960; words appear 742 / 1012 / 1413 ms after they end. The model's internal chunk is fixed at 320 ms — only the feed changes, so only $\alpha C$ moves | `sherpa-onnx 1.13.8` + the model (a few hundred MB, downloaded by `fetch`); reads `w03_d3_blank_heatmap/runs/rehearsal/` | CPU; tested on Apple silicon |
| [Demo 3 · Whisper's cross-attention heads: attention ≠ alignment](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos/w04_d3_attention_heads) | p45–p47 | Whisper small transcribes the same sentence correctly; all 144 cross-attention heads are laid out and classified by a stated criterion. Rehearsal: band 26, flat 86, stare 3, other 29; 114 of 144 heads put more than half their weight on the 24 s of padding after the audio. OpenAI's ten alignment heads (a code comment, not a paper) are boxed — 7 of them are bands, 19 bands are not on the list — and the word timestamps are recomputed from them by DTW and laid over W3's CTC spikes: a median offset of +0.107 s | `torch 2.14.0` + `transformers 5.17.0` + `openai/whisper-small` (≈ 1 GB, downloaded by `fetch`); CPU, `attn_implementation="eager"` | any laptop |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 27.0, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock` and `model.lock`. Menus and labels are in Chinese; the keys are listed in each README.

## References
- Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser & Polosukhin, **Attention Is All You Need**, NeurIPS 2017 (arXiv:1706.03762)
- Gulati et al., **Conformer: Convolution-augmented Transformer for Speech Recognition**, Interspeech 2020, pp. 5036–5040 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2020-3015; arXiv:2005.08100) — read this for the module-by-module breakdown and the ablation
- Dai, Yang, Yang, Carbonell, Le & Salakhutdinov, **Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models beyond a Fixed-Length Context**, ACL 2019, pp. 2978–2988 (DOI 10.18653/v1/P19-1285) — the source of the relative-position score decomposition and segment-level recurrence; the Conformer's self-attention reuses it
- Graves, **Sequence Transduction with Recurrent Neural Networks**, arXiv:1211.3711 (2012; ICML 2012 Representation Learning Workshop) — the original RNN-T paper; **this week's $\alpha$ / $\beta$ notation and conventions follow it**
- He et al., **Streaming End-to-end Speech Recognition for Mobile Devices**, ICASSP 2019 (arXiv:1811.06621) — the evidence for the RNN-T becoming the on-device streaming workhorse
- Zhang, Lu, Sak, Tripathi, McDermott, Koo & Kumar, **Transformer Transducer: A Streamable Speech Recognition Model with Transformer Encoders and RNN-T Loss**, ICASSP 2020 (arXiv:2002.02562)
- Chen, Wu, Wang, Liu & Li, **Developing Real-time Streaming Transformer Transducer for Speech Recognition on Large-scale Dataset**, ICASSP 2021 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP39728.2021.9413535; arXiv:2010.11395) — implementation details of the chunk-wise mask with Transformer-XL-style history; the mask in this week's maths follows it
- Shi, Wang, Wu, Yeh, Chan, Zhang, Le & Seltzer, **Emformer: Efficient Memory Transformer Based Acoustic Model for Low Latency Streaming Speech Recognition**, ICASSP 2021, pp. 6783–6787 (DOI 10.1109/icassp39728.2021.9414560; arXiv:2010.10759) — the memory bank, and right context that does not leak across layers
- Zhang, Chen, Yu, Yao, Khudanpur & Glass, **Highway Long Short-Term Memory RNNs for Distant Speech Recognition**, ICASSP 2016 (arXiv:1510.08983) — the source of latency-controlled BLSTMs (stated in the abstract); the historical member of the four streaming families
- Yao, Guo, Yang, Kang, Kuang, Yang, Jin, Lin & Povey, **Zipformer: A Faster and Better Encoder for Automatic Speech Recognition**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.11230) — the current efficient-encoder design; **not** a paper about bounding KV state
- Kuang, Guo, Kang, Lin, Luo, Yao & Povey, **Pruned RNN-T for fast, memory-efficient ASR training**, Interspeech 2022, pp. 2068–2072 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2022-10340; arXiv:2206.13236) — the memory wall and pruning with a linear joiner; the abstract names character-level Chinese vocabularies explicitly
- Yu et al., **FastEmit: Low-Latency Streaming ASR with Sequence-Level Emission Regularization**, ICASSP 2021, pp. 6004–6008 (DOI 10.1109/icassp39728.2021.9413803; arXiv:2010.11148) — emission delay and gradient reweighting
- Xu, Jia, Majumdar, Huang, Watanabe & Ginsburg, **Efficient Sequence Transduction by Jointly Predicting Tokens and Durations**, arXiv:2304.06795 (2023) — TDT, the transducer variant used by the Parakeet models; if Demo 2 uses `parakeet-mlx`, note that it is not a standard RNN-T; cited as a preprint
- Chan, Jaitly, Le & Vinyals, **Listen, Attend and Spell**, ICASSP 2016 (arXiv:1508.01211) — the starting point of AED, used to contrast non-monotonic alignment
- Chorowski, Bahdanau, Serdyuk, Cho & Bengio, **Attention-Based Models for Speech Recognition**, NIPS 2015 (arXiv:1506.07503) — degradation of content-only attention on long (ten-times repeated) utterances, and the source of location-aware attention
- Radford, Kim, Xu, Brockman, McLeavey & Sutskever, **Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision**, ICML 2023, PMLR 202:28492–28518 (arXiv:2212.04356) — Whisper; the model used in Demo 3
- The `_ALIGNMENT_HEADS` comment in `whisper/__init__.py` of OpenAI's `openai/whisper` source: "cross-attention heads that are highly correlated to the word-level timing" — **a source-code comment, not peer-reviewed literature**; the source for "even the authors trust only a handful of heads" in Demo 3
- **JM3** Ch 7 *Transformers and Pretraining*, Ch 16 *Automatic Speech Recognition* (2026-08-19 release)
- The systems side of KV caches and inference efficiency (further searching): *efficiently scaling transformer inference KV cache*, *multi-query attention memory bandwidth*
- SSMs / Mamba applied to speech: *Mamba speech recognition streaming*, *state space model audio*
- Streaming attention-based encoder–decoders: *monotonic chunkwise attention MoChA*, *triggered attention streaming*
